To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the formation of networks is positively affected by the provision of information by an employer, the quality of an intermediary, and by the individual’s subjective concern with the topic of occupational pensions.

(1) transaction cost theory and information search theory can be combined successfully in order to explain the formation and structure of information networks; (2) transaction cost theory provides an important contribution to explaining the formation of information search networks; (3) the employer's provision of information about pensions is a key factor explaining the formation and structure (size) of information search networks.

the transaction costs of information search, provision of information from the employer, quality and trustworthiness of the intermediary, as well as individual concern with the topic, increase the likelihood and number of network partners.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of information in the formation of social capital.
the role of information networks for employee participation in occupational pensions.
the role of information networks for the diffusion of knowledge and the formation of individual preferences.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the formation of networks is driven by the desire for better information and the desire for information about a particular topic.
the transaction cost approach provides a good explanation for the formation of networks.
information networks on occupational pensions are a good way to reduce transaction costs and to increase participation in pension plans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more the transaction cost is reduced and the more the quality of the information is improved the more employees are willing to participate in a pension network.

the more the employee is interested in the topic of occupational pension, the more information he or she will search for and the more network contacts he or she will establish to obtain information on this topic.
transaction costs are important for network formation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the employer is a key player in increasing the participation in networks for information on occupational pension plans.
transaction costs are a major determinant of information network formation.
transaction cost theory and network formation theory are useful to explain the formation and size of information networks on occupational pensions.
